title: Ch1: Notcurses goals -- 24-bit color, thread-safe, full Unicode; designed to replace NCURSES for modern TUI apps
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch10: Lines support color interpolation (lerping) -- hline_interp/vline_interp lerp between two channel pairs across the line length, useful for gradient borders
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: TUI minimum requirements -- input from keyboard/mouse, config menus, watching system events, safe synchronized access to graphics without wasteful polling or undue latency
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch10: Box drawing uses 6 cells (4 corners + hline + vline) with ctlword bitmask controlling which sides/corners draw and which get gradient interpolation. NCBOXGRAD_* bits enable per-side lerping. cells_rounded_box helper loads the nice curved Unicode chars
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch10: ncplane_gradient fills a rect with a single EGC in a 4-corner color gradient. ncplane_highgradient doubles vertical resolution using half-blocks. ncplane_polyfill_yx does flood fill. ncplane_erase resets plane framebuffer AND egcpool (faster after heavy use)
author: Robert Grayson

title: Appendix B: GPU terminals (alacritty, kitty) scale nearly flat with window size; xterm shows ~67% runtime increase over same range, near-quadratic. VTE scales poorly at large geometries. For a diff viewer, GPU-accelerated terminal performance matters at scale.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Terminal = line discipline + two buffers (input buffer for user events, output buffer for display). TUI freely moves cursor around rectilinear display vs CLI scrolling region
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch10: Staining (ncplane_stain) changes colors on existing cells WITHOUT changing glyphs or attributes. ncplane_format changes attributes without changing glyphs or colors. Alternative: overlay a transparent-glyph plane with desired colors on top for a 'moving stain' effect
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch10: ncblit_rgba/ncblit_bgrx blast raw pixel data onto planes -- every 2 input rows become 1 terminal row using half-blocks. No scaling built in. This is the foundation of all multimedia rendering
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: TUI advantages over GUI -- smaller memory/disk footprint, potentially less latency, more portable. But limited resolution, monospaced fonts reduce text space, must design for constraints
author: Robert Grayson

title: Appendix B: xterm with TrueType fonts pegs CPU via Xorg -- bitmapped fonts cut Xorg usage from 60%+ to under 20%. Font rendering is the dominant bottleneck for terminal display performance, not escape sequence parsing.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Terminal types -- hardware terminals, OS consoles, terminal multiplexers (tmux/screen/mosh with memory-persistent virtual terminal), and terminal emulators (virtual terminal atop GUI)
author: Robert Grayson

title: Appendix A: DEC VT heritage -- xterm slowly acquired VT100/VT220 features, every terminal claims 'ANSI' or 'VT100' compliance but these are NOT the same thing. VTE (GNOME/GTK3) underpins dozens of terminals. The terminfo database (maintained with ncurses by Dickey) is the authoritative source for terminal capabilities.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch11: Multimedia pipeline is open->decode->render loop. Scaling happens at decode time (can't rescale after). ncvisual_open_plane creates a plane sized to media dimensions. NCSCALE_NONE=exact, NCSCALE_STRETCH=fill, NCSCALE_SCALE=aspect-fit
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch6: Terminal modes -- canonical (cooked) buffers til newline, cbreak disables line buffering but keeps Ctrl+C, raw mode disables all preprocessing requiring userspace emulation of signals
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch3: Direct mode vs fullscreen -- direct mode styles printf output, no explicit render step, coexists with stdio. Use for non-interactive colorized output. Cannot discover terminal default RGB colors
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch11: ncvisual_stream handles the decode-render loop with timing from the media. timescale param controls speed (0.1=10x fast, 10=10x slow). streamcb callback runs per-frame; return non-zero to abort. ncvisual_simple_streamer is the default callback that renders+subtitles
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch3: Direct mode can open /dev/tty separately from stdout, allowing concurrent Notcurses display while piping stdout to another process (how notcurses-pipe works)
author: Robert Grayson

title: Appendix C: Linux console only supports 256/512 char fonts (PSF format), downsamples RGB to far fewer colors, and is missing rounded/double box-drawing chars. A TUI diff viewer targeting the raw Linux console would need fallback glyphs and a reduced color palette. Terminal emulators under X/Wayland are strictly more capable.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch6: TERM and COLORTERM env vars -- TERM must be correct (misinformation rampant), set COLORTERM=truecolor or 24bit for RGB support. terminfo is the abstraction layer for all escape sequences; never hardcode escapes
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch11: Sprites = new plane with transparent base + drawn content on top. Transparency lets background show through. Hit detection via ncplane_at_yx. For animation cycles, use one plane per frame and toggle visibility (used in luigi demo)
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch11: ncvisual_render accepts begy/begx/leny/lenx for rendering a sub-region of decoded frame. Used for parallax scrolling and zoom effects (eagle demo). Most efficient way to do scrolling over large images
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch6: Control sequences and sessions -- ESC (0x1b) introduces all ANSI sequences, CSI is ESC[ (0x27 0x5B). Only foreground process group can read terminal; background reads get SIGTTIN. SIGINT/SIGQUIT delivered to foreground group only
author: Robert Grayson

title: Appendix B: xterm flame graph shows massive time in recv()/writev() for X protocol messages -- this explains both poor scaling and high Xorg CPU load. GL-based terminals (alacritty, kitty) bypass X rendering pipeline entirely, doing their own GPU compositing. Bytes emitted are equal across terminals; the bottleneck is rendering, not I/O.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch3: Threading in direct mode -- terminfo lookups are read-only/safe, but fprintf to same FILE* has no ordering/atomicity guarantees. Multiple threads writing same FILE* must serialize. Read-only functions are free to call concurrently
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4: Fullscreen mode CRITICAL -- cannot use stdout/stderr to same terminal while active, will corrupt display. If logging to stderr, redirect it elsewhere. notcurses_refresh() syncs physical screen after corruption. Bind Ctrl+L to refresh
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch12: notcurses_getc returns char32_t (UTF-32 codepoint). NULL ts=block forever, zero ts=nonblock, nonzero ts=timeout. Returns 0 on timeout, -1 on error. ncinput struct gets codepoint + keyboard modifiers + cell coordinates. Input is per-codepoint not per-EGC
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch7: EGCs are the atoms of character graphics -- each cell holds one Extended Grapheme Cluster. Wide chars (CJK etc) occupy 2 cells; placing anything atop either half obliterates the whole wide char. A plane partially obstructing a wide glyph prevents it rendering entirely
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch12: Mouse requires explicit notcurses_mouse_enable(). Events: one for press, one per cell moved while held, one for release. NCKEY_RESIZE is synthesized and pushed to input queue on SIGWINCH. Non-Unicode keys (arrows, F-keys, mouse) use NCKEY_* constants from Unicode Private Area-B
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4: Alternate screen -- clears on entry, output not appended to scrollback, cleared on exit. Standard plane always exists, matches terminal size, cannot be destroyed/moved/resized by user. Must call setlocale(LC_ALL, "") before notcurses_init()
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch7: Half-block pixel trick -- U+2580 UPPER HALF BLOCK with fg+bg colors gives 2x vertical resolution with 1:1 aspect ratio. Smart impl replaces matching-color half blocks with FULL BLOCK + single fg, or space + single bg. This is how notcurses blits images
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch12: Widgets do NOT auto-handle input. Input queue is per-notcurses-context, not per-plane. Pattern: get input -> check your own handlers -> call widget_offer_input() in focus order -> if returns true, input consumed. Widget consume != widget acts (external control flow stays with caller)
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4: Render pipeline is 3 phases -- (1) RENDER: solve each cell by walking z-ordered planes top-to-bottom, (2) RASTERIZE: serialize only damaged cells to buffer, (3) WRITE: single write to terminal. Only damaged cells emitted, skipping undamaged saves ~95% bandwidth on partial updates
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch12: Terminal is in cbreak mode (input available immediately, no newline wait). Only one thread may call input functions at a time. Input can be called concurrently with output/read-only functions. sigset_t param controls signal masking during ppoll
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch7: UTF-8 is the only sane encoding -- ASCII maps 1:1 to first 128 UTF-8 chars, NUL-terminated C strings are valid UTF-8, self-synchronizing mid-stream. Max 4 bytes per codepoint. Always interoperate in UTF-8. Braille patterns U+2800 give 8x resolution (2x4 per cell) for graphing
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch7: Emoji pitfalls in TUI -- complex emoji EGCs (ZWJ sequences, skin tone modifiers) can decompose into multiple glyphs if font lacks support, destroying geometry for rest of line. Console fonts especially bad. Variation selectors U+FE0E/FE0F switch text/emoji presentation
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4: Performance rules -- hide planes at bottom behind opaque plane (not offscreen), keep planes no larger than needed, hold styling constant across horizontal stretches. Pathological case: per-cell RGB color changes. RGB change=14 bytes, palette=6 bytes, default=2 bytes overhead per cell
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch13: Selector widget -- auto-sized ncplane with infinite scroll, title riser optional. Options can be added/removed while active (even the selected one). ncselector_offer_input handles mouse clicks, scroll wheel, arrows, pgup/pgdown. Caller handles selection/cancellation logic
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4: Threading CRITICAL -- Notcurses does NO internal locking. notcurses_render() must mutually exclude ALL other mutating functions. Concurrent ops on DIFFERENT planes are safe (except z-axis changes). A function is only a reader if its ncplane arg is const. ncplane_destroy() changes z-ordering
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch13: Menu widget -- horizontal bar on top/bottom row. Can be hidden by default (hiding option). Auto-resizes on SIGWINCH. ncmenu_offer_input handles mouse hover/click, arrow keys, escape to roll up. ncmenu_selected returns current item + optional shortcut ncinput
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch13: Reel widget -- infinite-scrolling cylinder of dynamically created/destroyed tablets. Each tablet has a tabletcb draw callback with cliptop bool for partial visibility. ncreel_touch marks tablet dirty; ncreel_redraw redraws all. Supports eventfd notification for nonblocking input patterns
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch8: Plane z-ordering and defaults -- planes are totally ordered on z-axis. New planes go to top. Standard plane always exists, matches rendering area, cannot be destroyed. Planes init with null glyph (glyph-transparent) but default colors (color-opaque). Set fg/bg TRANSPARENT on base cell to let lower planes show through
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4: notcurses_render() can block for arbitrary time if terminal buffer fills. Cannot assume render corresponds to displayed frame -- terminal may batch-read multiple renders. Signal handlers auto-registered for SIGABRT/SIGINT/SIGQUIT/SIGSEGV to call notcurses_stop()
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch13: All widgets are just ncplanes -- movable on z-axis, can coexist. Widget styling via channel pairs in options structs (opchannels, descchannels, titlechannels, boxchannels, bgchannels etc). Reusable architecture pattern: options struct -> create -> offer_input -> selected -> destroy
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch8: Cell structure is 16 bytes -- gcluster (uint32, inline ASCII <128 or bias-128 index into per-plane egcpool) + attrword (uint32, style bits + palette indices) + channels (uint64, fg/bg RGB + alpha + flags). Egcpool can grow to 32MiB; unsafe to copy cells between planes due to pool indices
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch5: Canonical event+render loop -- (1) lay down essential screen elements, (2) discover initial state, (3) LOOP: watch for input/system events, perform mutual exclusion, manipulate ncplanes, call render(), (4) terminate. Font aspect ratio ~0.5 so use 2 rows per game-row, 4 cols per game-col
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch8: Alpha blending modes -- OPAQUE (default, stops rendering), TRANSPARENT (skip this plane), BLEND (weighted RGB mix, only works with RGB not palette/default), HIGHCONTRAST (fg-only, auto white/black for readability vs bg). Channel starts TRANSPARENT during render, solved when OPAQUE reached
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch8: Palette-indexed color saves bandwidth -- palette index requires much less escape sequence bytes than full RGB. Terminal palette size from 'colors' terminfo capability (typically 256). Palette can be reprogrammed if 'ccc' capability present. Default colors needed for terminal transparency effects
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch8: Threading with planes -- lock against concurrent plane access. notcurses_render() must be called from single thread. Use pthread_mutex around shared plane state. For periodic tasks (animations), spawn thread with timer, lock/unlock around plane operations and render calls
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch14: Demo walkthrough -- run at 80x45 min, need 24-bit color. Key demos: Intro (lerps+gradients+fades), Trans (transparency modes), Grid (max RGB density benchmark), Jungle (palette cycling for low-bandwidth animation), Fallin (many planes + introspection)
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch14: Tetris render pattern -- main thread loops on getc(blocking=true), timer thread calls MoveDown via sleep_for. Mutex protects shared state. Speculative move + InvalidMove check + rollback is the core movement validation pattern. ncplane_at_yx reflection used instead of maintaining separate state (DRY)
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch14: Tetris architecture -- stdplane for background, board plane for game area, curpiece plane for active tetrimino, score plane for text. Separate planes enable: trivial resize (just move planes), collision detection via translate+reflection, z-axis tricks for pause (move stdplane to top to hide game)
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch5: Plane coordinates are relative to the plane not the terminal. Cursor auto-advances on putchar/putegc. For multicolumn grapheme clusters cursor advances multiple columns. New planes start cursor at origin. Use ncplane_translate() to convert coords between planes
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch14: Tetris piece placement uses ncplane_mergedown to fuse piece plane onto board plane. LockPiece scans for cleared lines, shifts rows down, applies ncplane_stain gradient that changes per level. Score multiplied by (level+1) with point table [50,150,350,1000] for 1-4 lines
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch5: Between render calls, freely move/reorder/create/write/destroy planes with no flicker or tearing -- last rendered frame stays on screen. Only call render() when your plane stack is ready. NCKEY_RESIZE synthesized on terminal resize
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch14: Tetris resize handling -- on NCKEY_RESIZE: verify geometry large enough (else pause), redraw background, move board to new bottom-center, move curpiece relative to board. Pause implemented by moving stdplane to z-top (opaque, hides everything) + pulsing 'Paused' overlay plane
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch9: Text output API families -- putsimple (ASCII), putwc (wchar_t), putegc (single EGC), putstr (string of EGCs), printf. All return columns written (negative on error). _yx suffix moves cursor first (-1 means dont move). _stainable suffix updates glyphs without changing style. Scrolling disabled by default
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch9: 64-bit channels layout -- upper 32 bits = foreground, lower 32 = background. Each 32-bit channel: bit 30 = not-default-color flag, bits 29-28 = 2-bit alpha, bit 27 = palette-index flag, bits 23-0 = 24-bit RGB. Bit 31 of each half marks wide-char status (managed by notcurses, never touch). HIGHCONTRAST forbidden on background alpha
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch9: 32-bit attrword layout -- upper 2 bytes are NCSTYLE bitmask (BOLD 0x40000, ITALIC 0x1000000, UNDERLINE 0x400000, REVERSE 0x200000, DIM 0x80000, BLINK 0x100000). Lower 2 bytes hold palette indices (bits 15-8 = fg palette idx, bits 7-0 = bg palette idx). Not all styles supported on all terminals; query with notcurses_supported_styles()
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch9: Three color modes in terminals -- (1) default fg/bg colors (user-configurable, needed for terminal transparency, cant be blended), (2) palette-indexed (less bandwidth, 'colors' terminfo gives size), (3) RGB TrueColor 24-bit (indicated by 'rgb' terminfo or COLORTERM env). Only RGB can be blended. Setting RGB auto-marks channel as not-default
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch3 Direct mode: ncdirect_init(NULL, stdout) for styled printf. No render step. Coexists with stdio. /dev/tty trick allows concurrent display output + piped stdout. Thread-safe for reads but FILE* writes need serialization. NCDIRECT_OPTION_INHIBIT_CBREAK to keep terminal in canonical mode.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4 Fullscreen: notcurses_init(NULL, stdout) with zero-initialized opts == defaults. MUST call setlocale(LC_ALL, '') first -- only US-ASCII and UTF-8 supported, returns NULL otherwise. notcurses_stop() must be called even on abnormal exit. Default signal handlers call stop() before propagating SIGABRT/SIGINT/SIGQUIT/SIGSEGV.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4 notcurses_options fields: termtype(NULL=TERM env), inhibit_alternate_screen(bool, wire to user config), retain_cursor(bool, default hidden), suppress_banner(bool, hides stderr diagnostics+shutdown stats), no_quit_sighandlers(bool), no_winch_sighandler(bool), renderfp(FILE* for debug output), margin_t/r/b/l(int, best-effort, recomputed on resize)
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4 Render pipeline 3 phases: (1) RENDER - solve each cell top-to-bottom through z-stack: EGC from first non-null plane, fg from first OPAQUE/default/palette fg, bg same. Once cell fully solved skip lower planes. (2) RASTERIZE - compare rendered vs internal framebuffer, skip undamaged rows, absolute cursor move to leftmost damage, emit EGCs+style escapes only when changed. (3) WRITE - collected into one big buffer, single write() to terminal.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4 Render costs: RGB color change ~14 bytes per escape, palette index ~6 bytes, default color reset ~2 bytes ('op' escape). For ASCII chars, RGB fg+bg = 2800% overhead per cell! Holding styling constant across horizontal stretch is critical. Most pathological: fg+bg RGB changes cell-by-cell. U+2588 FULL BLOCK treated as all-fg, U+0020 SPACE as all-bg -- notcurses emits whichever needs fewer bytes.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4 Performance inversely proportional to: (color changes across screen) * (planar depth before opaque found) * (UTF-8 bytes per glyph) * (screen geometry). notcurses_render() can block if terminal doesn't consume buffer fast enough. Hide planes behind opaque plane rather than moving off-screen. Planes should be no larger than necessary.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch4 Threading: NO internal locking. notcurses_render() mutually excludes ALL other mutations (plane writes, z-order changes, stats). ncplane_at_yx() is a WRITER (touches egcpool) even though it looks like a read. Function is reader ONLY if ncplane arg is const. Concurrent ops on DIFFERENT planes are safe UNLESS changing z-order. ncplane_destroy() updates z-order so conflicts with ncplane_move_top().
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch5 Event loop pattern: (1) lay down essential screen elements (2) discover initial state, add to display (3) LOOP: thread watches for input, other threads collect system events (4) threads perform mutual exclusion (5) threads manipulate ncplanes (6) single thread calls notcurses_render() (7) process terminates. Between renders, freely move/create/destroy/write planes -- no flicker, last frame persists.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch5 Plane transparency: by default planes obstruct COLOR but not GLYPHS. Unwritten cells have null EGC (transparent glyph) but opaque default fg/bg. Fix: set base cell fg alpha to NCALPHA_TRANSPARENT via ncplane_set_base(n, '', 0, channels) where channels has both fg+bg alpha transparent. Without this, overlapping planes show 'bounding box' color artifacts.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch5 Input+timer pattern: main thread blocks on notcurses_get_blocking(), releases mutex before blocking, reacquires after. Timer thread runs clock_nanosleep() loop for periodic updates (rotation, animation). Both lock against shared ncplane state. Or use timerfd_create()+epoll for single-thread IO multiplexing.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch6 Terminal modes: CANONICAL (default) -- line-buffered, Ctrl+C=SIGINT, Ctrl+Z=SIGTSTP, Ctrl+\=SIGQUIT. CBREAK -- no line buffering but signals still work, process input char-by-char while keeping Ctrl+C. RAW -- all signal translation disabled, Ctrl+C must be emulated in userspace. Notcurses uses cbreak or raw internally.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch6 TERM/COLORTERM: TERM set by terminal emulator, forwarded by ssh (except with -T). Must be correct terminfo entry. COLORTERM must be manually set for 24-bit TrueColor. These are the two most important env vars for TUI apps. Bad TERM = garbage output, missing features, poor performance.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch7 Wide chars: occupy 2 cells, cannot print half. Placing ANY char atop a wide char's left or right half OBLITERATES the entire wide char. Wide char on last column: obliterates content but is not itself rendered. A plane partially obstructing a wide glyph prevents it from rendering entirely. wcwidth() determines width but fonts can disagree.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch7 EGC (Extended Grapheme Cluster): the atomic unit of display. One EGC per cell. Can be multi-codepoint (base + combining marks). Example: e + combining acute = one EGC in one cell. Notcurses stores EGCs in egcpools when they exceed 4 bytes. ASCII chars stored directly in cell's gcluster field (< 128).
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch7 Half-block pixel trick: U+2580 UPPER HALF BLOCK + U+2584 LOWER HALF BLOCK give 2x vertical resolution. Each cell becomes 2 pixels (fg=upper, bg=lower). With 1:1 cell aspect ratio (~0.5 font aspect), this yields approximately square pixels. Braille patterns (U+2800-U+28FF) give 8x resolution (2x4 dots per cell) but only 2 colors per cell.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch7 UTF-8: ASCII-compatible (first 128 bytes identical), NUL-safe (0x00 only encodes NUL), self-synchronizing (can find char boundaries from any position), max 4 bytes per codepoint, preserves memcmp() sort order. All multibyte sequences have high bit set. strcmp/memcmp work for equality. Notcurses requires UTF-8 locale.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch7 Emoji hazards: ZWJ (Zero Width Joiner) sequences combine multiple emoji into one glyph but terminal support varies wildly. Variation selectors (VS15/VS16) switch between text and emoji presentation. Flag sequences use Regional Indicator pairs. Skin tone modifiers. All of these can break geometry assumptions. Avoid emoji in TUI grid layouts.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch8 ncplane creation: ncplane_create(parent, &opts) with .y/.x/.rows/.cols. New planes always at TOP of z-axis. Standard plane: cannot destroy/move/resize, always matches terminal size, origin at (0,0). ncplane_move_top/bottom for absolute z-moves, ncplane_move_above/below for relative. Destroying a plane updates z-order.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch8 Cell struct (16 bytes): gcluster(uint32 - ASCII<128 inline, >=128 is biased index into egcpool), attrword(uint32 - style bits), channels(uint64 - fg upper 32 + bg lower 32). Multicolumn EGC at cell N overrides cells N+1..N+width-1 (zeroed out). Cells are per-plane due to egcpool refs -- unsafe to copy between planes.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch8 Base cell: rendered wherever plane's gcluster==0 (null EGC). Set via ncplane_set_base(ncp, channels, attrword, egc). Erasing plane does NOT reset base cell. This is how you make transparent planes (set base alpha to TRANSPARENT) or colored backgrounds (set base bg). Base cell applies to glyph, attributes, AND colors.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch8 Alpha modes (4 levels per fg/bg channel): OPAQUE - use this color, search terminates. TRANSPARENT - skip this channel, continue to lower plane. BLEND - weighted average with computed color so far (only works with RGB). HIGHCONTRAST - compute fg that contrasts against computed bg (fg only). Default colors cannot be blended.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch8 Palette: notcurses_palette_size() returns count. Palette-indexed color uses ~6 bytes per change vs ~14 for RGB. palette256 API allows reprogramming terminal palette (requires 'ccc' terminfo cap). Fading: ncplane_fadeout/fadein with callback per step. Pulsing: ncplane_pulse() oscillates between full and faded states.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch9 Text output: ncplane_putchar_yx (ASCII), ncplane_putsimple_yx (1-byte UTF-8), ncplane_putwc_yx (wchar_t), ncplane_putegc_yx (UTF-8 EGC string), ncplane_putstr_yx (UTF-8 string), ncplane_printf_yx (formatted). Cursor auto-advances by glyph width. Coordinates relative to plane origin. Use mbswidth() not strlen() for column counting.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch9 Channels (64-bit): bits 63-32 = fg channel, bits 31-0 = bg channel. Each 32-bit channel: bit 31-30 = alpha (2 bits), bit 29 = palette-indexed flag, bit 28 = default-color flag, bits 27-25 = reserved, bit 24 = wide-char flag, bits 23-0 = RGB (8r+8g+8b). Three color modes: default (cheapest bandwidth), palette-indexed (~6B), RGB (~14B).
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch9 NCSTYLE bits (32-bit attrword): NCSTYLE_STANDOUT, NCSTYLE_UNDERLINE, NCSTYLE_REVERSE, NCSTYLE_BLINK, NCSTYLE_DIM, NCSTYLE_BOLD, NCSTYLE_INVIS, NCSTYLE_PROTECT, NCSTYLE_ITALIC. Not all terminals support all styles. Check with notcurses_supported_styles(). Set/add/remove via ncplane_styles_set/on/off.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch10 Drawing: ncplane_hline/vline for lines with lerped colors. ncplane_box for rectilinear boxes (6 cells: ul/ur/ll/lr/hline/vline + ctlword bitmask for which sides to draw). ncplane_rounded_box/double_box helpers. ncplane_gradient fills rect with EGC, interpolating 4 corner colors (ul/ur/ll/lr). ncplane_highgradient uses half-blocks for 2x resolution gradients.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch10 Stain+format: ncplane_stain(n, ymax, xmax, ul, ur, ll, lr) changes CHANNELS over rectangular region WITHOUT touching glyphs or attributes. ncplane_format(n, ymax, xmax, attrword) changes ATTRIBUTES without touching glyphs or colors. These enable highlighting, gradients over existing content. ncplane_polyfill fills contiguous same-colored region. ncplane_erase clears all cells to null EGC (but NOT base cell).

title: Ch10 Blitting: ncblit_rgba/bgrx takes raw pixel data, converts to half-blocks (2 input rows per terminal row, fg=upper pixel, bg=lower pixel). ncvisual_from_rgba for in-memory images. title: Ch1: Actor is state + mailbox + handlers (reiterated)
description: First concept beat: reiterates the Ch 0 three-part actor definition (private state nothing outside can touch, a mailbox queue of messages, handlers that run one at a time pulling off the mailbox). Important to restate because Ch 1 is where the reader first sees concrete syntax, and they need the mental model fresh.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: Hewitt 1973 paper as foundation
description: Explicitly cites Hewitt's 1973 actor-model paper: every piece of state is owned by some small independent process, the only way to touch it is via messages. Everything Erlang, Elixir, Akka, Pony, and Blimp do with actors derives from this. Sets up credibility and lineage before asking the reader to trust that the syntax makes sense.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: become is Hewitt's original primitive, not mutation
description: Hewitt emphasized 'become' in the original paper. An actor doesn't mutate state; it becomes its next state. The old version still existed and the runtime remembers it. Blimp keeps this word because Blimp keeps the model. Sets up the Ch 1 introduction of become and foreshadows time-travel debugging in later chapters.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: Ruby-surface Elixir-data-model influences
description: Quick syntax orientation: Blimp's surface looks like Ruby with do/end blocks, optional parens, almost-English sentences. The data model is Elixir's: immutable values, pattern matching, pipes, atoms. Readers from either background will feel something familiar.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: The five-line Bike shell
description: Shows the smallest Bike actor that means anything:  with two state fields (id, status) and no handlers yet. This is the reader's first concrete piece of Blimp. The chapter proceeds to dissect each line.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: actor Name do...end declares a template
description: The  block declares a template, not a live instance. When the reader writes , the runtime clones the template. Capital-letter names are types, lowercase names are variables/functions. This naming convention is how Blimp distinguishes types from values at parse time.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: state field syntax — name, type, default all required
description: State fields have three parts: a name (id), a type (String), and a default value ("unknown"). Both the type and the default are REQUIRED. Design reasons: the type gives the runtime and reader the shape at a glance (can't discover mid-flight that id is an integer), and the default means  with zero args always works (no constructors, no 'forgot to initialize' bugs). An actor starts working the moment it's born.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: :: (two colons) for default assignment — why not =
description: The default-assignment operator is . Two colons. It has to be two colons because a single colon already means something else: a single colon in front of an identifier makes an atom (like :available). To keep atoms readable without ambiguity, default assignments got their own operator. Minor but frequently asked question about Blimp syntax.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: Atoms — :available, :rented, :ok, and why
description: Atoms are Blimp's interned symbols. Same thing as Ruby symbols or Elixir atoms: a constant whose identity is its name, compared by identity rather than content, cheap at runtime. Used everywhere in Blimp for states, tags, and message names. Readers coming from either Ruby or Elixir will recognize them immediately.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: 'Atoms show up everywhere' — taxonomy of atom uses
description: Atoms appear in three load-bearing roles: the messages you send (), the states an actor can be in (:available, :rented, :broken), and the tag at the front of tagged tuples like {:ok, X} or {:error, reason}. Readers should get comfortable with atoms early because they'll keep seeing them.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: Handler state-field scope — no self, no this, just id
description: Inside a handler body, state fields are in scope as ordinary variables. You read them by name: uid=501(robertgrayson) gid=20(staff) groups=20(staff),12(everyone),61(localaccounts),79(_appserverusr),80(admin),81(_appserveradm),33(_appstore),98(_lpadmin),100(_lpoperator),204(_developer),250(_analyticsusers),395(com.apple.access_ftp),398(com.apple.access_screensharing),399(com.apple.access_ssh),400(com.apple.access_remote_ae),702(com.apple.sharepoint.group.2),701(com.apple.sharepoint.group.1) in the handler body is the same uid=501(robertgrayson) gid=20(staff) groups=20(staff),12(everyone),61(localaccounts),79(_appserverusr),80(admin),81(_appserveradm),33(_appstore),98(_lpadmin),100(_lpoperator),204(_developer),250(_analyticsusers),395(com.apple.access_ftp),398(com.apple.access_screensharing),399(com.apple.access_ssh),400(com.apple.access_remote_ae),702(com.apple.sharepoint.group.2),701(com.apple.sharepoint.group.1) declared as a state field above. You don't write self.id or this.id. This is a deliberate departure from OOP habits; handlers read more like pure functions over state than methods on an object.

title: Ch1: reply — what it is, what happens without it
description: sends a value back to whoever sent the message. Every handler can call reply to produce a return value. If a handler doesn't call reply explicitly, you still get a default reply (nil or the next state depending on context), but being explicit is clearer to read and easier to test. The tutorial uses explicit reply throughout.

title: Ch1: spawn with field overrides — syntax and rationale

title: Ch1: Why become exists — Hewitt's original formulation
description: Deep-dive on the become primitive. Rather than mutating state (bike.status = 'rented'), Blimp declares 'become status: :rented'. Two reasons: (1) Hewitt's original paper framed a handler's output as 'a reply plus the actor the actor should become next' (an entire next-actor, not a diff); (2) immutable snapshots give you mailbox-based mutual exclusion (preview of Ch 2) AND time-travel debugging (preview of later chapters).

title: Ch1: become semantics — 'Read it out loud: Become, status is rented'
description: Concrete sentence reading of the become statement: 'Become: status is rented.' A bike that had status == :available a moment ago is now a bike that has status == :rented. The old version still exists in the actor's history, but from this line on the new version is what the runtime hands to any incoming message. Handler runs atomically, no mid-update visible.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: compute / transition / communicate rhythm
description: Three-beat rhythm Blimp's design doc (docs/lang_design/core-language-feel.md) calls out for handlers: compute (pipes transform data), transition (become transforms the actor), communicate (reply speaks to the caller). The :rent handler is empty-compute, then become, then reply :ok. Naming the rhythm helps readers spot the shape when they see it in later chapters' more complex handlers.

title: Ch1: :ok convention — success reply, pairs with :error
description: The atom :ok is a Blimp convention for 'handler did what was asked, nothing else to hand back.' Pairs with {:ok, something}, :error, {:error, reason}. Callers use the tag to branch on success vs failure via pattern matching, just like Elixir. Load-bearing convention even though it's not a type.

title: Ch1: The five-line Bike shell
description: Shows the smallest Bike actor that means anything: an 'actor Bike do ... end' block with two state fields (id, status) and no handlers yet. This is the reader's first concrete piece of Blimp code. The chapter then dissects each of the three pieces in the block (the actor keyword line, the first state declaration, the second state declaration) before introducing handlers.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: actor Name do...end declares a template
description: The 'actor Bike do ... end' block declares a template, not a live instance. When the reader writes 'spawn Bike', the runtime clones the template. Capital-letter names are types; lowercase names are variables and functions. This capitalization convention is how Blimp distinguishes types from values at parse time, which matters for message passing and actor references later.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: state field syntax - name, type, default all required
description: State fields have three parts: a name like 'id', a type like 'String', and a default value like the string "unknown". Both the type and the default are REQUIRED. The type gives the runtime and reader the shape of the actor at a glance so you cannot discover mid-flight that 'id' was secretly an integer. The default means 'spawn Bike' with zero arguments always works, so no constructor boilerplate and no 'I forgot to initialize this field' bugs. An actor starts working the moment it is born.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: :: (two colons) for default assignment, why not =
description: The default-assignment operator is the two-colon sequence, not a single equals sign. It has to be two colons because a single colon already has meaning in Blimp: a single colon in front of an identifier makes an atom, like the atom spelled ':available'. To keep atoms readable without ambiguity, default assignments got their own operator. A small syntactic decision, but worth calling out because readers frequently ask why it is not just '='.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: Atoms show up everywhere, taxonomy of uses
description: Atoms appear in three load-bearing roles in Blimp code: the messages you send (such as sending ':rent' to a bike), the states an actor can be in (like ':available', ':rented', ':broken'), and the tag at the front of tagged tuples like a success tuple or an error tuple. Readers should get comfortable with atoms early because they will keep seeing them in every subsequent chapter.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: Exercise step 1, reply with state
description: First piecemeal exercise step: fill in the ':id' handler so it replies with the bike's id. The reader replaces the stub's 'reply :TODO' with 'reply id'. Teaches the handler block syntax ('on :msg do ... end'), the fact that state fields are in scope inside the handler body as ordinary variables with no 'self' or 'this' prefix, and the 'reply' primitive. After this step the 'reports its id' test goes green.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: reply primitive, what it is and what happens without it
description: The 'reply' statement sends a value back to whoever sent the message. Every handler can call reply to produce a return value. If a handler does not call reply explicitly, you still get a default reply (nil or the next-state depending on context), but the tutorial uses explicit reply throughout because it is clearer to read and easier to test. Handler return values become the value of the corresponding '<-' send expression at the call site.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: spawn with field overrides, syntax and rationale
description: 'spawn Bike' creates a live instance using all declared defaults. 'spawn Bike, id: "b-001"' overrides the id field at spawn time. Any state field can be overridden this way, and fields you do not mention keep their declared defaults. The syntax replaces the constructor boilerplate common in OOP: you get direct field naming at the call site, and an actor template you never need to instantiate manually.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: Variables hold references, actors live in runtime registry
description: After 'b = spawn Bike, id: "b-001"', the variable 'b' holds a reference, not the actor itself. Actors do not live in your expression scope; they live in the runtime registry. When you write 'b <- :id', the runtime looks up 'b', finds the actor in the registry, delivers the message, and evaluates to the reply. Two variables can point at the same actor, and actors can outlive the variable that first named them. This is load-bearing for later chapters on supervision and addressing.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: <- send operator, blocking in today's Blimp
description: The '<-' send operator reads as 'send this message to that actor, wait for the reply, evaluate to the reply.' In today's Blimp every send blocks until the reply returns. That is a real constraint of the current runtime, not a design end-state, and it will matter in later chapters when we need to drive an always-running loop (the Clock in chapter 7) via external ticks since we cannot schedule async sends from within Blimp itself.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: Exercise step 2, on :status
description: Second piecemeal exercise step: fill in the ':status' handler so it replies with the bike's current status. Same shape as the ':id' handler from step 1: 'on :status do reply status end'. This step is pure reinforcement, not new concepts. The only difference is the field type (Atom instead of String). After this step the 'starts available' test goes green.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch1: Exercise step 3, on :rent with become
description: Third piecemeal exercise step: fill in the ':rent' handler. The reader writes 'become status: :rented' followed by 'reply :ok'. This is the first handler that actually changes state, so it introduces the become keyword in practice after the concept was set up. After this step the 'rent flips status to :rented' test goes green.

Nothing new to learn, just reinforces the become/reply pattern with the opposite target state. After this step the 'return flips status back' test goes green, and all four tests are green.
author: Robert Grayson

description: Chapter closes by pointing out a bug. If the reader sends ':rent' twice in a row to the same bike, both times succeed: status stays :rented and reply stays :ok. In a real bike share this means two people think they rented the same bike. The fix is chapter 2's guarded ':rent' handler, which also motivates the chapter-2 punchline about why Blimp needs no locks (the mailbox-as-lock argument).
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch 2: State, become, and the free lock
description: Chapter 2 extends the Chapter 1 Bike by adding multi-clause handlers with guards, tagged-tuple replies, a new ':broken' state, and the punchline argument for why Blimp does not need mutexes. The chapter opens on the double-rent bug from Chapter 1, introduces multi-clause dispatch and 'when' guards, teaches the {:ok, ...} / {:error, ...} convention from Elixir, adds ':return' and ':report_broken' handlers, and then delivers the 'why the lock is free' section that ties the safety to two language rules: actors have mailboxes, and handlers run to completion (BEAM-style scheduling).
author: Robert Grayson

rationale: Ch 2 adds guards and explains the free-lock argument
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: The Ch 1 double-rent bug as motivation
description: Chapter opens with the bug from chapter 1: two ':rent' messages in a row both succeed, status stays :rented, reply stays :ok. In a real bike share that means two people think they rented the same bike. The chapter exists to fix this bug, and to use that fix as the vehicle for explaining why Blimp does not need mutexes.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: The usual mutex fix and its fragility
description: The typical imperative fix for 'only one rental succeeds' is to wrap the read-and-write in a mutex so concurrent callers cannot both see :available at the same time. The downside: if you forget the lock, the race ships and the bug shows up three weeks later in prod. The chapter references this pain to set up the Blimp alternative.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Blimp has no mutexes, this chapter explains why none are needed
description: Explicit claim up front: Blimp does not have mutexes. By the end of the chapter the reader will see why it does not need them. This framing lands the punchline at the end with more impact, because it has been promised from the opening.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Additions in this chapter
description: The chapter adds four handlers to the Bike: a guarded ':rent' that only succeeds when the bike is available, a fallback ':rent' that refuses with an error tuple, a ':return' that flips the bike back to available, and a ':report_broken' that marks a bike for the mechanic. Plus the associated concepts needed to understand those handlers.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Multi-clause handler syntax
description: You can define 'on :rent' more than once with the same message atom but different clauses. When a :rent message arrives, Blimp tries the clauses top to bottom; the first clause whose guard matches is the one that runs. A clause with no 'when' always matches, so it works as the catch-all fallback.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Multi-clause dispatch rule, first match wins
description: Dispatch rule: Blimp tries handler clauses from top to bottom, and the first clause whose guard matches is the one that runs. If you have written Erlang or Elixir function heads, this is exactly the same shape. If you have not, read it as 'try the clauses in order, first match wins.'
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Design decision reference - multi-clause pattern matching is foundational
description: Links to the early Blimp design decision (node 15 in the graph): pattern matching and immutability are core to the language, which meant borrowing the Erlang/Elixir function-head shape for defining behavior instead of having one monolithic handler body with branching inside. Putting the branching in the dispatch itself lets the runtime see it, which will matter for future optimizations and introspection.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Guards with when, syntax
description: The 'when <expression>' bit after the message pattern is a guard. It is a boolean expression with access to the actor's state fields and any parameters the message carries. If it evaluates truthy, the clause matches and runs. Guards let multi-clause dispatch inspect state and input values without needing full if/else inside the handler body.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Guard language restrictions and why
description: Guards are intentionally kept simple: comparisons, arithmetic, boolean operators, but no arbitrary function calls. That restriction keeps guards predictable and lets the runtime fast-path the check without worrying about side effects leaking through during dispatch. Readers coming from general-purpose if-statements need to understand this limitation.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Exercise step 1, guarded :rent with become and :ok
description: First piecemeal step: fill in the guarded ':rent' clause with 'become status: :rented' and 'reply :ok'. The guard filters for 'only when status is :available', the become commits the new state, the reply answers the sender. After this step the tests 'first rent returns :ok' and 'first rent flips status to :rented' go green. Two of seven.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Tagged tuples convention
description: Blimp, like Elixir, wraps success and failure values in tagged tuples. The canonical shapes are the atom :ok alone for simple success, a two-tuple with :ok and a payload for success with data, the atom :error alone for simple failure, and a two-tuple with :error and a reason atom or string for failure with context. The atom at the front of the tuple is the tag, and callers typically pattern-match on it.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Pattern-match on tagged tuples in case statements
description: Shows the canonical consumer-side pattern: a 'case' over a reply from an actor, with one branch for :ok and another for {:error, _}. This is exactly how Elixir code handles results, and it is why the tagged-tuple convention is load-bearing even though it is not a type enforced by the compiler.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Convention not type, flexibility and payoff
description: The {:ok, ...} and {:error, ...} shape is a convention, not a compiler-enforced type, so you can use any shape you want. The payoff of following the convention is that every caller already knows how to branch on your reply. Blimp does not force it because Blimp avoids forcing things, but downstream code is dramatically easier if you stick to it.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Errors as values via reply, not exceptions
description: Blimp does not have try/catch inside handlers. For unrecoverable failures, there is the 'bubble' mechanism (taught in chapter 5). For expected failures like 'the bike is not available right now,' the answer is to return a tagged tuple. Errors in Blimp are values that flow back through the reply, not exceptions that you have to catch. This is a fundamental difference from Java-style exception handling and worth highlighting.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Exercise step 2, fallback :rent with error tuple
description: Second piecemeal step: fill in the fallback ':rent' clause so it replies {:error, :unavailable}. No become in this one; a rejected rental does not change the bike's state, it just says no. After this step the tests 'second rent returns error tuple' and 'refused rent does not change status' go green.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Exercise step 3, :return mirror
description: Third piecemeal step: fill in the ':return' handler as a mirror of the rent from chapter 1: 'become status: :available' then 'reply :ok'. Nothing new to learn, same pattern as Ch 1's :rent with the opposite target. After this step 'after return, can rent again' goes green.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Third state :broken, atoms let you invent new states
description: After ':available' and ':rented', real bike shares also have bikes with flat tires and bikes in the mechanic's queue. In a language with enums, adding a state would mean editing a type somewhere and remembering to handle the new variant everywhere it is matched. In Blimp, status was typed as Atom, and any atom you have not used yet is already a valid status. No declaration needed: 'become status: :broken' just works.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Dispatch reuses automatically - fallback :rent already rejects broken
description: When the bike is broken, the guard on the first :rent clause ('when status == :available') evaluates to false, so the fallback clause runs and replies {:error, :unavailable} automatically. No new handler needed for the broken case; the multi-clause dispatch already knows what to do. Elegant side effect of letting the dispatch do the branching instead of an if-statement inside one big handler body.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Exercise step 4, :report_broken
description: Fourth and final piecemeal step: fill in ':report_broken' with 'become status: :broken' and 'reply :ok'. After this step the 'broken bike refuses rent' test goes green, which makes all seven tests green and the exercise complete.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Python mutex example setting up the free-lock argument
description: The chapter's payoff section begins by showing what the Python equivalent would look like: a function that reads bike.status, checks for 'available', writes 'rented', and returns. Two threads running this race trivially, which is the motivation for a mutex around the read-and-write. The example makes concrete what 'free lock' is freeing us from.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Blimp version shown with no mutex, no race claim
description: The chapter shows the Blimp version (two clauses, guard plus fallback) and asserts 'no mutex, no synchronized, no locks anywhere, and also no race.' The following paragraphs unpack why the assertion is true, not just convenient.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Reason 1 for free lock - the mailbox serializes messages
description: First reason the lock is free: every actor has a mailbox, and the actor pulls messages off one at a time in arrival order. While the first ':rent' handler is running, the second ':rent' is sitting in the mailbox waiting its turn. It cannot race the first one because it is not running yet. This is the core property that eliminates shared-memory contention.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Reason 2 for free lock - handlers run to completion (BEAM scheduling)
description: Second reason: a handler runs to completion before the next one starts. Blimp's scheduler is modeled on Erlang's BEAM, which means actors get preempted between messages, not mid-handler. By the time the second :rent is pulled off the mailbox, the first one has already committed its become, and the guard 'when status == :available' on the first clause sees the post-become state, evaluates to false, and the fallback clause runs.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: No inconsistent window - states are both fully-formed
description: There is no inconsistent 'both see available' window at any point. The actor has no window of inconsistency at all, because no other code can observe or modify the actor's state while a handler is running. The previous state and the next state are both valid, fully-formed versions of the actor, and the transition from one to the other is atomic.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: 'Safe concurrency by construction' phrase
description: The phrase actor-model enthusiasts love is 'safe concurrency by construction.' Read it as: you did not do anything to earn the safety. The mailbox is the lock and the handler is the critical section, and both came with the actor the moment it was defined. No imperative-style mutex, no synchronized, no lock-free data structure, just the two language rules working together.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Summary - seven green tests, zero mutexes, zero shared-memory hazards
description: What the reader built in this chapter: a Bike that refuses double rentals, refuses to be rented when broken, lets you take it out of service and put it back in. Seven green tests. Zero mutexes. Zero shared-memory hazards. The whole thing comes from two language rules working together: each actor has a private mailbox, and handlers run to completion. Neither rule is something the reader added to the code; they come from defining an actor in the first place.
author: Robert Grayson

title: Ch2: Ch 3 preview - actors talking to each other
description: Chapter closes with a preview of chapter 3: adding a DockingStation that holds a pile of bikes and hands them out on request, while each individual Bike still owns its own state. Once there is more than one actor in the system, the only way they can interact is by sending each other messages, and the reader will start to feel why that constraint actually buys you something instead of just feeling like a limitation.
